title: Demonstrate an understanding of vine pruning

lessons.title: Why and when we prune vines
lessons.html:
Why and when we prune vines

Pruning means cutting away part of the vine. Grapes grow on new green shoots, and these shoots grow from buds on last season's wood. If we do not prune, the vine becomes a thick bush with many small, poor bunches, and it is hard to spray and pick.

Reasons for pruning

  • To keep the frame shape: trunk, cordons and spurs.
  • To control how many buds are left, and so how many bunches grow.
  • To balance crop and growth, so the vine can ripen its grapes properly.
  • To keep the canopy open for sun and air, which reduces disease.
  • To remove dead, diseased and damaged wood.

When to prune

The main pruning is done in winter (roughly June to August in the Western Cape), when the vine is dormant and has no leaves. You can see the wood clearly. Pruning too early or too late can affect budding, so follow the farm's programme. Blocks are often pruned in a set order, and cultivars that bud early may be pruned later to reduce frost risk.

Words to know

  • One-year-old wood (cane): brown, smooth wood that grew last summer. It carries the buds for this season's crop.
  • Older wood: darker, rough wood of the cordon and trunk.
  • Spur: a cane cut back short, leaving a few buds.
  • Bearer: another name for a spur or cane left to carry the crop.
  • Water shoot: a shoot growing from old wood; usually has little fruit.

Tools

Sharp, clean secateurs (pruning shears); loppers or a pruning saw for thick wood. Keep a sharpening stone with you. Clean tools between blocks if your supervisor asks, to avoid spreading disease.

lessons.title: How to prune a spur-pruned vine safely
lessons.html:
How to prune a spur-pruned vine safely

Many South African wine vineyards on a cordon trellis are spur pruned. Some cultivars or systems use cane pruning instead; your supervisor will show you which method to use in each block.

Steps for spur pruning

  1. Look first. Stand in front of the vine and look at the whole cordon. Plan which canes to keep.
  2. Remove dead and damaged wood first.
  3. Choose the bearers. On each spur position, pick a good cane: pencil thick, healthy, growing upwards, close to the cordon. Choose the lowest good cane so the spur does not climb higher every year.
  4. Cut back to the right number of buds. Usually two buds per spur, but follow the farm's instruction for the cultivar.
  5. Remove the other canes on that spur position cleanly, close to the old wood.
  6. Space the spurs evenly along the cordon. Remove spurs that are crowded, and leave a water shoot only if it is needed to fill a gap or renew a spur.
  7. Remove suckers on the trunk.

Making a good cut

  • Cut through the node above the last bud you keep, or about a finger width above it, as the farm teaches.
  • Slope the cut away from the bud so water runs off.
  • Cut cleanly. Do not crush or tear the wood.

After pruning

Pull the cut canes out of the wires and leave them in the middle of the row for mulching or chopping. Some farms seal large cuts to protect against wood diseases; follow the farm's practice.

Safety

  • Always keep your free hand behind or above the cut, never in front of the blades.
  • Wear gloves and safety glasses; canes can spring back at your eyes.
  • Carry secateurs closed or in a holster.
  • Keep a safe distance from the next worker.
  • Do not use loppers above your head; stand so cut wood falls away from you.

Key points

  • Pruning keeps the frame, controls crop and opens the canopy.
  • The main pruning is done in winter when the vine is dormant.
  • Keep a healthy, low cane at each spur position and cut it to the set number of buds.
  • Make clean, sloping cuts and space spurs evenly.
  • Keep your free hand away from the blades and wear safety glasses.

quiz.question: When is the main pruning of vines done?

options.text: In winter when the vine is dormant
In midsummer when grapes are ripe

quiz.question: Where do this season's grapes grow from?

options.text: Shoots from buds on last season's wood

quiz.question: Which cane should you choose as a spur?

options.text: The highest cane, far from the cordon
A healthy, pencil-thick cane low and close to the cordon

quiz.question: Why should the cut slope away from the bud?

options.text: So water runs off and away from the bud

quiz.question: Where should your free hand be when you cut with secateurs?

options.text: Holding the cane between the blades
Behind or above the cut, away from the blades

quiz.question: If vines are not pruned, they make many small, poor bunches.
